subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors of anterior pituitary cells that alter hormone production or compress surrounding structures. Their size and secretory profile dictate clinical presentation and management.

sections.p: Pituitary adenomas arise from monoclonal expansion of hormone‑producing cells. They are classified by size (<1 cm micro, ≥1 cm macro) and by the hormone they secrete or by being non‑functioning.
Normal anterior pituitary cells synthesize peptide hormones from pre‑prohormones, regulated by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting factors and feedback loops.
b: GH: GHRH ↑ → GH ↑ → IGF‑1 from liver
TSH: TRH stimulates TSH; thyroid hormone provides negative feedback

sections.p: Feedback loops keep hormone levels within narrow ranges; disruption by an adenoma leads to autonomous secretion or loss of regulation.
b: Loss of dopamine inhibition → prolactinoma hypersecretion
TSH‑secreting adenoma bypasses thyroid hormone feedback

sections.p: Genetic mutations (e.g., MEN1, GNAS) drive clonal growth. Excess hormone causes systemic effects; mass effect compresses optic chiasm and cavernous sinus.
b: MEN1 mutation → multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1

sections.p: Patients present with hormone‑related syndromes or visual field loss. Early recognition prevents irreversible organ damage and guides targeted therapy.

t.b: Is hyperprolactinemia present? Elevated >200 ng/mL confirms prolactinoma; normal level suggests non‑functioning lesion.
Is GH excess? Elevated IGF‑1 with age‑adjusted reference indicates acromegaly; normal IGF‑1 argues against GH‑secreting tumor.
What is the size and extension? Shows micro vs macroadenoma and optic chiasm compression; if unavailable, CT can detect large lesions.

sections.p: Focus on hormone profiles, imaging findings, and syndromic clues. Remember MEN1 association and that non‑functioning adenomas present mainly with mass effect.
b: Macroadenoma >1 cm → visual field testing mandatory
Prolactin >200 ng/mL usually indicates prolactinoma, not stalk effect
GH‑adenoma: IGF‑1 elevation + lack of GH suppression on oral glucose tolerance test

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision or visual field defects
Rapidly worsening endocrine symptoms (e.g., thyrotoxicosis, adrenal crisis)

faq.q: Why do some pituitary adenomas cause low hormone levels?
faq.a: Large non‑functioning adenomas compress normal pituitary tissue, leading to hypopituitarism.

faq.q: Can a prolactinoma be treated without surgery?
faq.a: Yes, dopamine agonists normalize prolactin and shrink the tumor in most cases.

faq.q: What is the link between pituitary adenoma and MEN1?
faq.a: MEN1 gene mutations predispose to multiple endocrine tumors, including prolactin‑, GH‑, and TSH‑secreting adenomas.

exam: Describe the hormonal feedback disruption in a GH‑secreting pituitary adenoma.
Interpret a serum prolactin level of 350 ng/mL in the context of a sellar mass.
Explain why bitemporal hemianopsia occurs in macroadenomas.
